analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: Despite 181 cosponsors and a discharge petition to force a floor vote, the bill sat in three House committees and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the legal ban on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and require the Interior Department to sell leases on the refuge's coastal plain, with the first sale at least 200,000 acres within 22 months. It includes environmental rules, a 12.5% royalty, limits on surface development to 2,000 acres, and protections for caribou calving and subsistence hunting, plus land transfers to Alaska Native corporations, impact aid for local communities, and a trust fund routing leasing revenue to alternative energy programs. It also shortcuts some normal environmental review: the Interior Department would not have to study a no-leasing alternative, public comments would be limited to a 20-day window, and lawsuits could only be filed in one appeals court, which would presume the department's analysis correct. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain access to a federal refuge that has been closed to leasing since 1980. The State of Alaska would receive 50% of leasing revenue, Alaska Native corporations would receive land conveyances and employment preferences, North Slope communities would get up to $11 million in impact aid, and federal alternative energy programs would receive a share of the remaining revenue through a new trust fund. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 1003 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, which prohibits producing oil and gas from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and directs the Interior Secretary to run a competitive leasing program on the refuge's coastal plain. [S2] [S3]
Requires the first lease sale within 22 months of enactment, offering at least 200,000 acres chosen for the greatest hydrocarbon potential, at a royalty of at least 12.5%. [S3]

Sends 50% of bonus, rental, and royalty revenue to the State of Alaska and directs the balance to a new ANWR Alternative Energy Trust Fund that funds programs under the 2005 energy law and the 2007 energy independence law. [S3]

Conveys surface land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and subsurface estate to Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, requires lessees to use best efforts to employ Alaska Natives, and creates an impact aid fund of up to $11 million for communities affected by development. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental risk of industrial development in a pristine wildlife refuge, including effects on caribou, polar bears, birds, and subsistence hunting by Alaska Natives. Any relief at the gas pump would depend on global oil markets, not on this lease program, and the bill narrows the public's ability to challenge the leasing decisions in court. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill shortens environmental review: the Interior Department would not have to analyze a no-leasing alternative under the National Environmental Policy Act, could consider only public comments filed within 20 days, and challenges would go only to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, where the department's analysis would be presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence. [S3]

Drilling in the coastal plain could harm wildlife, habitat, and the subsistence hunting that Alaska Natives rely on; the refuge's coastal plain is the calving ground of the porcupine caribou herd and home to denning polar bears. The bill attempts to manage this with a 'no significant adverse effect' standard, seasonal drilling limits, a 2,000-acre surface footprint cap, and special areas, but it also makes the Interior Secretary's authority to close lands to leasing exclusive to this act. [S3]

The title promises price reduction, but new oil from any single field reaches a global market; there is nothing in the bill that guarantees lower gasoline prices for consumers, and the bill actually prohibits exporting oil produced under the leases. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine compromise within the pro-drilling position: it carries more environmental protections and local benefit-sharing than many earlier ANWR opening bills, including a surface footprint cap, seasonal limits, reclamation liability, impact aid, and an alternative energy trust fund. But the core trade is unchanged: the public would trade a permanently protected refuge for revenue and uncertain, likely marginal, future oil supply, while the procedural shortcuts on environmental review and judicial challenge reduce the public's ability to hold the process accountable. The bill never became law, so none of these trade-offs were tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees that never reported it, and a discharge petition meant to force it out of committee and onto the floor never got it a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on May 21, 2008, with Rep. Roscoe Bartlett of Maryland as the other original sponsor. [S1] [S3]

The House referred it to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Science and Technology committees, which in turn referred it to three subcommittees; none of the committees ever marked it up or reported it to the floor. [S5]

On July 30, 2008, Rep. Michele Bachmann filed a motion to discharge the committees from further consideration, the first step of a discharge petition that can force a bill to the floor if a majority of House members sign. [S5]
The bill had 181 cosponsors, 176 Republicans and 5 Democrats, but never received a committee or floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S4] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge remained closed to oil and gas leasing, which is the outcome conservation advocates and opponents of drilling in the refuge wanted; the oil and gas industry gained no access to the coastal plain. Members who supported drilling gained nothing from this Congress, though the issue remained live in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of drilling in the refuge

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 176 of 199 House Republicans cosponsored, against 5 of 233 House Democrats, and no Democratic committee ever advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would open a wildlife refuge that has been legally closed to leasing since 1980, handing oil companies access to federal oil under competitive leases at a 12.5% royalty. The public cost is environmental risk in a pristine refuge and a shortened, court-shielded review process, while any consumer price relief is uncertain because oil trades on a global market.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill conveys land title to these corporations, requires lessees to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives, and funds community impact aid. Many of their members also depend on the caribou herd and subsistence resources that drilling could affect.

industries.industry: North Slope local governments and communities
industries.note: The bill creates an impact aid fund of up to $11 million and community service assistance for local governments bearing the burden of development, while also obligating them to live with the industrial activity the bill authorizes.
The bill creates the ANWR Alternative Energy Trust Fund, routing a share of oil leasing revenue to authorized alternative energy and efficiency programs under the 2005 and 2007 energy laws.
